newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS-French government sticks to EMU election promises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French government sticks to EMU election promises.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government on Monday did exactly what it said it would do in its election campaign -- it pushed hard to get its vision of a single currency accepted without derailing the whole project.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his partners in the European Union that the new government -- pledged to turning Europe's focus to growth and jobs -- was not ready to accept a stability pact limiting budget deficits after the launch of the euro in 1999.
But he told a news conference that France was committed to launching economic and monetary union in 1999. "The French government is utterly determined to launch EMU on time."

Strauss-Kahn said France did not want to renegotiate the pact, but wanted time to consider it, and look at ways of reinforcing political co-ordination inside the euro zone to seek policies encouraging growth and lowering unemployment.

He said he thought it would be hard to reach an accord in time for a summit of EU leaders in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17, noting that new Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was not due to make his keynote policy speech to parliament until June 19.

His statement threw France's EU partners into turmoil -- not because of the substance of the French demands -- but because of the risk that political momentum towards a single currency could be slowed by failure to approve the accord in Amsterdam as planned.

Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told reporters there was a large degree of consensus around the French demands, noting there were provisions in the Maastricht Treaty for reinforcing political co-ordination.
"I think that we have quite a great consensus already...but the time constraint is a bit of a problem," he said.

At the heart of the issue is a drive by the new French government to ensure that the monetarist vision of Europe enshrined in the future European Central Bank is balanced by a political vision where a European economic government would seek common policies geared to growth and jobs.
Strauss-Kahn said fiscal discipline and price control were essential, but Europe also needed growth and employment.
"Because if we need credibility in the eyes of financial markets, we also need credibility among the peoples of Europe," he said.

Strauss-Kahn did not spell out exactly how France wanted to complete the stability pact, though he cited two articles in the Maastricht Treaty -- articles 102a and 103 -- which allow for greater co-ordination of economic policies.

Former European Commission president Jacques Delors said in an interview with Belgian daily Le Soir on Monday that this greater policy co-ordination could be included in a protocol to the stability pact.
"We are seeking the application of the (Maastricht) Treaty, notably the provisions which aim to create an economic pillar alongside the monetary pillar," Delors said.

"Article 103 of the Maastricht Treaty foresees that every year the European Council adopts common policies on economic issues," Delors said. "We need to spell out how this will be done in a protocol which will complete the stability pact."
The aim would be to set up a forum associating labour and social affairs ministers with finance ministers to draw up common policies for growth inside the euro zone.

France's previous centre-right government tried, and failed, to get its EU partners to accept the idea of an economic government. It settled in the end for an informal "stability council" to coordinate policies.

But the Socialist party, swept to power in a surprise election victory earlier this month, accused the previous government of not fighting hard enough to get France's vision of Europe accepted abroad.
One official said during the campaign that Jospin was prepared to go through a period of high tension to get France's views accepted -- a prediction borne out by Monday's events.
The Socialist party has caught the crest of the wave in pushing for more emphasis on growth and jobs -- taking a similar line to that of Britain's new Labour Party government.

The fact that France's EU partners were willing on Monday to contemplate greater economic policy co-ordination, after dismissing the demands of the previous government, suggested the new administration might be more successful at pushing France's demands.
But economists said France would have to steer a fine line to push its demands without alienating its main ally Germany.

Jospin and French President Jacques Chirac were due to meet German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday for a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France, which will also be attended by finance and foreign ministers from both countries.
